This report in front of committee today is seeking approval of the draft 2024 to 2035
major capital funding plan.
The steps towards creating this plan have been in progress and through numerous
council approvals over the past year.
This included July 18, 2022 with direction to bring back a 24 to 35 major capital prioritization
process, September 19, 2022 approval of the process and guiding principles to develop
the prioritization list and March 29th, 2023 approval of the 24 to 35 major capital
prioritization list.
This report is the final step in approving the draft plan which administration will use
to create future budget submissions.
In development of the draft funding plan, the administration utilized the following steps
to determine which projects would receive funding.
Number one, projects that have been submitted for other levels of government funding and are
aligned on this plan for the city's share were prioritized first.
Number two, city council provided previous direction that this plan would be utilized to repay
a portion of the 2022 emergency snow event as such the administration has allocated $5 million
towards this purpose.

impacting response times were viewed to be funded early in this plan.

listing.

projects in the first six years of the plan to be included.
When developing the plan, it became clear that forecasting out further than this time frame
was difficult due to unknowns surrounding government funding in order to avoid significant future
changes.
The administration is recommending that the back half of this plan be developed as more details
are known about future government programs.
Overall, the first six years of this plan include $162 million in total projects, utilizing
63.1 million in city funding.
This plan assumes approval of many of the city's funding applications to provincial and federal
governments.

City's solicitors office has presented a number of reports to Council regarding a comprehensive
protocol policy for City Council.
This report is another possible component of that policy, and this report is regarding
lobbying of members of Council, and is an issue that Council asked us to consider in reviewing
a components of a new comprehensive protocol policy.
Lobbies are usually those who represent a business or financial interest and are communicating
with public office holders in an attempt to influence policy and decisions.
Attached as Pintex 1 to the report is a jurisdictional scan of other municipalities.
There are varying ways that lobbying is dealt with across Canada at the municipal level.
Quebec has provincial legislation and a provincial registry.
Ontario has legislation that requires Toronto to adopt a lobbyist registry, but is optional
for other municipalities.
Some additional cities in Ontario have adopted a registry, but many have not.
Some other jurisdictions in Canada, municipalities have developed voluntary registries.
However, many municipalities do not have a registry.
Three options are outlined in the report.
We are recommending option 1 or the status quo.
Under this approach, we would not make any changes from the city's current approach in this
area.
At this time, the administration does not see the need for a registry.
There are provisions in the Code of Ethical Conduct that would apply to lobbying related
activities.
The city has also established meeting protocols that are managed by the city clerk's office
to ensure requests from community groups or private individuals are handled in a transparent manner.
This process will be codified in the new comprehensive protocol policy.
The city also has general provisions in our procurement documents that put obligations on
bidders to prohibit lobbying and requires bidders to engage in ethical behavior.
Neither is municipal lobbying, neither is a municipal law being registered required by provincial
legislation in Saskatchewan.
The only municipalities that have mandatory lobbyist registries are those that have provincial enabling
legislation.
Further, there is a cost to maintaining a registry.
At this time, the administration views the current approach as sufficient.
However, this issue can be revisited if the landscape changes in Saskatchewan.
